Requirements: 1. The text contains page numbers in square brackets, such as [01], [02], etc. - These must be passed through unchanged. - Each page number must appear in exactly the same position in the translation as in the source. - The number of page markers in the output must match the input exactly.
2. Personal names, place names, titles, and other proper nouns should be rendered in Hànyǔ Pīnyīn with tone marks.
3. Do NOT transcribe the full Classical Chinese text into Pinyin.
4. Do NOT include explanatory notes, annotations, or commentary — output only the English translation.

p.seg: "Forest of Laughter": A man from Wú arrived in the capital.
His host served him làosū (a dairy product),
but he didn't know what it was.
He forced himself to eat it,
and upon returning home, he vomited and became severely ill.
He said to his son:
'Even if I died alongside those bumpkins,
I would have no regrets;
however, you must be careful about this in the future.'
*Lei Ju* 72, *Yu Lan* 858.
A man from Tàiyuán had a fire break out at night.
He rushed to save his belongings,
intending to retrieve a bronze spear,
but mistakenly grabbed a flatiron.
He was greatly astonished and exclaimed,
saying to his son:
'How strange! (These two words are present in the *Lei Ju* citation.)
The fire hasn't even reached it yet,
but the spear has already lost its legs from being burned!'
*Shu Chao* 135, *Lei Ju* 72, *Yu Lan* 757.
A certain Mr. Jiǎ (recorded as a man from Wèi in *Guang Ji*) fell suddenly ill at night
and ordered his servant to drill for fire.
The night was dark and overcast, and he couldn't get a flame.
Jiǎ催促 him urgently (recorded as "pressing him quite urgently" in *Guang Ji*).
The servant angrily said:
'Sir, your责难 is utterly unreasonable!
It's as dark as lacquer now; why don't you hold a torch to light my way?
Then I could find the fire-drilling tools (as in *Lei Ju* 80 and *Yu Lan* 869) easily.'
Kǒng Wénjǔ heard of this and said: 'One should责难 others appropriately.' *Guang Ji* 258.
Someone went to offer condolences and also wanted to bring a gift to assist the family.
He asked someone: 'What kind of thing can I give?'
The person replied: 'Money, cloth, grain, or silk—whatever you have!'
So he brought a hú of beans and placed them before the filial son, saying:
'I have nothing else, so I offer this hú of soybeans (these fourteen characters supplemented from *Guang Ji*) to help.'
The filial son cried out, 'What am I to do?'
The visitor thought he was asking about the beans,
and replied: 'They can be cooked into饭!'
The filial son cried out again, 'I am destitute!'
The visitor said (in *Guang Ji*: The filial son cried, '孤穷, what am I to do?' The visitor said, 'Make...?' The filial son cried again, '孤穷!' The visitor said):
'If you've just now (Wáng Lìqì edition: become) destitute, I should naturally send another hú.'
*Lei Ju* 85, *Guang Ji* 262.
Shěn Héng's younger brother, Shěn Jùn, styled Shūshān,
was well-reputed,
but his nature was frugal and stingy.
When Zhāng Wēn was sent as an envoy to Shǔ, he bid farewell to Jùn.
Jùn went inside for a long time,
then came out and said to Wēn:
'I just now selected a bolt of cloth,
intending to give it to you, but I couldn't find a coarse one.'
Wēn praised his ability to openly admit his fault. The above also appears in *Lei Ju* 85, *Yu Lan* 820, *Xu Tan Zhu* 4.
Also, once when traveling along the shore of Tài Lake,
he had an attendant fetch some salt water;
afterwards, regretting that it was too much, he ordered him to pour some back.
Soon after, he himself felt ashamed and said:
'This is my inborn nature!' *Guang Ji* 165.
Zhào Bógōng (recorded as Wēng in *Lei Lin*) was a large, corpulent man.
One summer day, he lay drunk.
His young grandson, several years old, climbed onto his belly to play
and inserted several plums (one source: eight or nine) into his navel.
When Bógōng woke up, he was completely unaware.
Several days later, he began to feel pain.
The plums had rotted, and juice flowed out.
Thinking it was a hole in his navel,
and fearing death, he summoned his wife and children to arrange family affairs.
Weeping, he told his family:
'My intestines are rotting, and I am going to die.'
The next day, a plum pit came out. Upon inquiry,
he learned it was the plums his grandson had inserted.
*Yu Lan* 371 and 966, *Yu Ji* 14, *Lei Lin Za Shuo* 10.
During Emperor Huán's time, someone resigned from his post as a clerk in a government office.
He asked someone to compose a memorial for him.
The person couldn't write it, so he told him:
'Previously, Gě Gōng from Liángguó was excellent at writing memorials.
You can simply copy one of his to use; no need to trouble yourself to write a new one.'
So the man followed this advice and copied a memorial,
but he didn't remove Gě Gōng's name.
The prefect was greatly startled and dismissed him without a reply.

Therefore, people of the time said: 'Though the memorial is skillfully made, one should remove Gě Gōng's name.' *Yu Lan* 496. Note: The commentary to the *Hòu Hàn Shū* biography of Gě Gōng states: Gě Gōng was skilled at writing memorials. Someone asked Gě Gōng for a memorial to present to another person. Gě Gōng wrote it for him. That person copied it but forgot to put his own name on it, and thus copied Gě Gōng's name as well and presented it. Therefore, people of the time said of him: 'Though the memorial is skillfully made, one should remove Gě Gōng's name.' Seen in *Forest of Laughter*, differing from the *Yu Lan* citation.
During the Hàn, the Minister over the Masses Cuī Liè appointed
Bào Jiān from Shàngdǎng as a clerk.
When about to have his audience,
Jiān worried he wouldn't know the proper etiquette,
so he asked someone who had arrived earlier about the仪式.
Someone happened to reply:
'Just follow what the master of ceremonies chants.'
When the audience began, the master of ceremonies chanted, 'Kě bài (You may bow),' and Jiān also said, 'Kě bài';
the master of ceremonies chanted, 'Jiù wèi (Take your position),' and Jiān also said, 'Jiù wèi.'
Then he put on his shoes and went to his seat.
When about to leave the mat, he didn't know where his shoes were.
The master of ceremonies said, 'Lǚ zhuó jiǎo (Shoes are on your feet),'
and Jiān also said, 'Lǚ zhuó jiǎo yě (Shoes are indeed on my feet).'
*Yu Lan* 499.
A man from Chǔ was carrying a pheasant. A passerby asked, 'What bird is that?'
The carrier deceived him, saying, 'A phoenix!'
The passerby said, 'I have long heard of the phoenix; now I truly see one.
Will you sell it?'
He said, 'Yes!'
The passerby then offered a thousand in gold, but the carrier refused. He asked to double the price, and then the carrier agreed.
Just as he was about to present it to the King of Chǔ, the bird died overnight.
The passerby didn't have time to regret his gold; he only regretted not being able to present it.
People throughout the state spread the story, all believing it was a real, precious phoenix that he had intended to present,
and the news reached the King of Chǔ.
The king was moved that he had wanted to present it to him.
He summoned the man and rewarded him richly,
exceeding ten times the price paid for the 'phoenix.' *Guang Ji* 461.
A man from the Táoqiū family in Píngyuán married a woman from the Mòtái family in Bóhǎi.
The woman was very beautiful and talented,
and they respected each other.
After she had borne a son, she returned to her娘家.
Her mother, Dīng shì, was elderly. When she went to see her daughter, she felt apprehensive (恐).
After the daughter returned (恐), she was sent away by her husband.
As the wife was about to leave, she asked for her fault.
Her husband said:
'When I saw your mother earlier,
her age and vitality had declined,
not comparable to former times.
I also fear that when you, my new wife, grow old, you will surely become like this!
Therefore I am sending you away;
there is truly no other reason.' *Yu Lan* 499.
A certain Mr. Jiǎ served as an assistant in a powerful official's residence, but he was utterly ignorant.
Whenever there were gatherings with musical entertainment, he would always participate;
but ashamed of his ignorance, when the courtesans performed songs
and others praised them, he would also imitate people, looking up and praising in agreement.
His contemporaries once had him act as host and also put him in charge of summoning the courtesans and guests.
Before the courtesan guests had assembled, he summoned a courtesan and asked in detail about the songs and tunes,
writing them down one by one on slips of paper placed under his handkerchief box.
There was already a medical prescription there. When the guests had gathered, he was asked to request songs.
He first took the notes he had written, but mistakenly picked up the prescription,
and said it was the song list, which included: 'Fùzǐ, three parts;
Dāngguī, four parts.'
He then said:
'Let's perform "Fùzǐ Dāngguī" to send off the guests.' The entire company burst into laughter. *Yu Lan* 568.
When southerners came to the capital, people would warn them:
'If you are given something to eat, just eat it; be careful not to ask its name!'
One such man went to his host's house. Upon entering the gate, he saw horse droppings and immediately ate them.
Finding the smell foul, he stopped.
Proceeding further, he saw worn-out straw sandals discarded by the road,
so he chewed on them too, finding them utterly impossible to swallow.
Turning to his companion, he said: 'Let's stop! One cannot believe everything people say.'
Later, visiting a high official, a feast was set for him (一引作饌).
Upon seeing it, he said: 'You are the first thing (一引作戒故昔物); I certainly should not eat you.'
*Yu Lan* 698 and 851.
Someone was making soup.
He tasted it with a ladle, found it lacking salt, and added some.
Later, he tasted again from the same ladle and still said the salt was insufficient.
He repeated this several times, adding over a shēng of salt.
The soup still wasn't salty,
and he found it very strange. *Yu Lan* 861.
Mr. Jiǎ bought meat and was passing through the city. He entered a latrine,
hanging the meat outside.
Mr. Yǐ stole it,
but before he could leave,
Jiǎ came out looking for his meat.
Yǐ then deceitfully put the meat in his mouth and said:
'If you hang it outside the door, how can you not lose it?
If, like me, you put the meat in your mouth, there would be no reason to lose it.' *Yu Lan* 862, *Shu Chao* 140.
Yáo Biāo and Zhāng Wēn both went to Wǔchāng.
They encountered Shěn Héng from Wúxīng by the riverbank, waiting for favorable winds.
Héng's provisions were exhausted, so he sent someone to borrow a hundred hú of salt from Biāo.
Biāo's nature was stern and upright.
Upon receiving the letter, he didn't reply but continued discussing with Wēn.
After a long while, he ordered his attendants:
'Pour a hundred hú of salt into the river.'
He then said to Wēn:
'It's not that I begrudge the salt;
I begrudge to whom it would be given!' *Guang Ji* 165, *Yu Lan* 865.
A poor man from Chǔ was reading the *Huáinánzǐ* and came upon the passage:
'The mantis watches the cicada, concealed by a leaf that can make it invisible.'
So he went under a tree and looked up to pick such a leaf.
A mantis was holding a leaf, watching a cicada.
He plucked it, but the leaf fell beneath the tree.
There were already many fallen leaves under the tree, and he couldn't distinguish which was the right one. So he swept up several dǒu of leaves and returned home.
He held up leaves one by one to conceal himself, asking his wife, 'Can you see me?'
At first, his wife always answered, 'I can see you.'
After a whole day, she grew weary and annoyed, and lied, saying, 'I can't see you.'
He was silently overjoyed. Taking the leaf, he went to the market and took people's belongings right in front of them.
The officers then arrested him and took him to the county office.
The county accepted his statement, and he explained the whole story from beginning to end.
The official laughed heartily and released him without punishment. *Yu Lan* 946.
During the Hàn dynasty, there was an old man who had no sons.
His family was wealthy, but he was frugal and stingy, wearing poor clothes and eating plain food.
He rose at dawn and rested late at night;
he managed his property and accumulated wealth insatiably, yet dared not use it for himself.
If someone came to him begging,
he would reluctantly go inside to fetch ten coins.
Walking from the hall, he would reduce the amount with each step, so that by the time he reached the outside,
only half remained. He would close his eyes and hand it to the beggar.
Immediately afterwards, he would嘱咐:
'I am exhausting my family wealth to support you; be careful not to tell others,
lest they imitate you and come!'
The old man soon died. His fields and houses were confiscated by the state,
and his goods and wealth filled the imperial treasury. *Guang Ji* 165.
There was a man A who wanted to visit the county magistrate. He asked the attendants, "What does the magistrate enjoy?"
Someone told him, "He enjoys the Gōngyáng Commentary."
Later, when he went in for an audience, the magistrate asked, "What books do you read, sir?"
He replied, "I only study the Gōngyáng Commentary."
The magistrate tested him, asking, "Who killed Chéntuō?"
After a long pause, man A replied, "I have truly never killed Chéntuō in my life."
The magistrate, realizing his mistake, then teased him further, saying:
"If you didn't kill Chéntuō, then who did?"
At this, he became terrified, ran out barefoot.
When people asked him the reason, he loudly exclaimed:
"When I met the magistrate, he immediately questioned me about a murder case.
After this, I simply dare not come again. I should only come out if I receive a pardon." From Extensive Records, scroll 260.
Man A and man B got into a fight.
Man A bit off man B's nose.
The officials wanted to decide the case.
Man A claimed that man B bit it off himself.
The official said, "A person's nose is high and the mouth is low; how could he reach to bite it?"
Man A said, "He stepped on a stool to bite it." From Extensive Records, scroll 262.
Man A's parents were alive. He went away to study for three years and then returned.
His maternal uncle asked him what he had gained from his studies,
and also inquired after his long-absent father.
He then replied:
"My thoughts for my uncle surpass those of Qín Kāng."
Afterward, his father scolded him:
"What good did your studying do?"
He replied:
"I lacked my father's instruction in my youth, so my studies were of no benefit." From Extensive Records, scroll 262.
Some country bumpkins wanted to go together to offer condolences, but none knew the proper etiquette.
One man said he was somewhat familiar with it,
and told his companions, "Just follow my lead."
When they arrived at the place of mourning,
the one who claimed prior experience went first, prostrating himself on the mat.
The others, one by one, piled on top of him, pressing down on his back;
The leader, annoyed, kicked and cursed, saying, "You idiots!"
The others also thought this was part of the proper ritual,
so they each kicked one another, saying, "You idiots!"
The last one was near the bereaved son.
He also kicked the bereaved son and said, "You idiot!" From Extensive Records, scroll 262.
There was a foolish son-in-law. When his father-in-law died,
his wife taught him how to perform the mourning rites.
On the way, he encountered a stream,
so he took off his socks to wade across,
but lost one sock.
Then he saw a turtledove in the woods calling, "Gūgū! Gūgū!"
He privately recited this sound and completely forgot the mourning ritual.
When he arrived, he stood on one foot with one sock on,
and tucked up the bare foot,
just saying, "Gūgū! Gūgū!"
The bereaved sons all laughed.
He then said, "Don't laugh! Don't laugh!
If you find my sock, please return it to me." From Extensive Records, scroll 262.
In Lǔ, there was a man carrying a long pole trying to enter the city gate.
First, he held it vertically—
it wouldn't go in.
He held it horizontally—
it also wouldn't go in.
He was at a loss for a plan.
Soon an old man arrived
and said, "I am not a sage,
but I have seen many things.
Why don't you saw it in half and then enter?"
So he followed the advice and sawed it. From Extensive Records, scroll 262.
A man from Qí went to a man from Zhào to learn to play the sè.
Before leaving, he glued the tuning pegs in place and then returned home.
For three years, he couldn't play a single tune.
The man from Qí found it strange.
When someone came from Zhào,
he asked him about it and only then realized the foolishness of the previous man. From Extensive Records, scroll 262.
In the state of Wú, there was a man named Hú Yōng,
who was very fond of women.
He married a woman named Zhāng,
and doted on her, never leaving her side.
Later, she died,
and Hú Yōng also passed away.
His family buried them together in the back garden.
After three years, when they went to move the burial,
they saw the grave mound had transformed into two figures;
often seen embracing as when they lay together.
People all laughed at this.
From Extensive Records, scroll 389.
A man from Hàn went to Wú.
The people of Wú served bamboo shoots.
He asked what they were.
They told him, "Bamboo!"
When he returned home, he boiled his bamboo bed mat, but it wouldn't cook tender.
He then said to his wife:
"Those crafty people of Wú
deceived me like this!" From the Bamboo Shoot Treatise, and Gànzhū Collection, scroll 11.
